figures.caption: Cholinergic and glutamatergic synapses: where cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine act.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left: acetylcholine released into the synapse is broken down by acetylcholinesterase, which donepezil blocks. Right: excess glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors; memantine blocks the open channel.

figures.caption: The four dopamine pathways and the effect of D2-receptor block in each.
figures.alt: Table-like diagram with four rows: mesolimbic, mesocortical, nigrostriatal and tuberoinfundibular pathways, their normal roles, and the result of D2 block: fewer positive symptoms, worse negative symptoms, extrapyramidal effects and raised prolactin.

figures.caption: Levodopa from gut to brain, with the sites of carbidopa, entacapone and MAO-B inhibitors.
figures.alt: In the periphery, levodopa is converted by AADC to dopamine (blocked by carbidopa) and by COMT to 3-O-methyldopa (blocked by entacapone). Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and brain AADC makes dopamine, which MAO-B breaks down; selegiline and rasagiline block this.

figures.caption: Serotonin and noradrenaline synapse: targets of the antidepressant classes.
figures.alt: Presynaptic neuron with MAO blocked by MAO inhibitors, SERT and NET blocked by SSRIs, SNRIs and TCAs, and the alpha-2 autoreceptor blocked by mirtazapine. A side note links alpha-1, H1 and muscarinic block to adverse effects.

figures.caption: Targets of antiseizure drugs at excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
figures.alt: Left: glutamate nerve ending with Na+ channels, the alpha-2-delta Ca2+ subunit and SV2A, and postsynaptic AMPA receptors, with the drugs acting at each. Right: GABA nerve ending with GABA transaminase blocked by valproate, the GABA-A receptor enhanced by benzodiazepines and phenobarbital, and thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels blocked by ethosuximide.

figures.caption: Sites of action of skeletal muscle relaxants from brain to muscle fibre.
figures.alt: A vertical chain: brain and brainstem, spinal cord, neuromuscular junction and muscle fibre, each linked to the drugs acting there: antispasmodics, antispastics, neuromuscular blockers and dantrolene.

figures.caption: The GABA-A receptor and the binding sites of GABA, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, barbiturates and flumazenil.
figures.alt: Top view of five subunits (two alpha, two beta, one gamma) around a chloride channel, with GABA sites between alpha and beta and the benzodiazepine site between alpha and gamma. A side panel summarises the action of each drug group.

figures.caption: Balanced anaesthesia: the five goals and the drugs that provide each.
figures.alt: A central hub labelled general anaesthesia linked to five boxes: unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, muscle relaxation and loss of autonomic reflexes, each with example drugs.

figures.caption: How a local anaesthetic crosses the nerve membrane and blocks the Na+ channel from inside.
figures.alt: Outside the nerve the drug exists as base and cation. The unionised base crosses the lipid membrane; inside, it becomes ionised and binds the inner side of the Na+ channel. Acidic tissue leaves more drug ionised outside.
